title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text: This page is a companion to Anisotropy and Whitening. It derives the whitening matrix and a few facts the main article uses. It assumes basic linear algebra (matrix product, transpose, eigendecomposition).

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Setup
We have \(N\) embeddings, stored as row vectors \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{1\times d}\). Define
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{x}_i, \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}) \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}.
\]
Each term \((\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\) is a \(d\times d\) outer product (a column times a row). \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is symmetric and positive semi-definite; we assume it is positive definite (all eigenvalues \(>0\), which needs enough data and no perfectly redundant coordinates).
We look for a \(d\times d\) matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) such that
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathbf{W}
\]
has mean \(\mathbf{0}\) and covariance \(\mathbf{I}\).

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
section: Step 1: mean and covariance of the transformed data
text:
Step 1: mean and covariance of the transformed data
Mean. \(\frac1N\sum_i \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = \left(\frac1N\sum_i \mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}\right)\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{0}\). Subtracting \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) already makes it zero for any \(\mathbf{W}\).
Covariance. Since the mean is zero,
\[
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
= \frac1N\sum_i \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\top\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i
= \frac1N\sum_i \mathbf{W}^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\mathbf{W}
= \mathbf{W}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{W}.
\]
So the requirement is the single matrix equation
\[
\mathbf{W}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{I}. \tag{1}
\]

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Step 2: diagonalise \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)
A symmetric positive definite matrix has an eigendecomposition (the spectral theorem; for such matrices it coincides with the SVD):
\[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top,
\]
where \(\mathbf{U}\) is orthogonal (\(\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}\)) and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\text{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d)\) with \(\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_d>0\).

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
The solution is not unique
If \(\mathbf{R}\) is any orthogonal matrix, then \(\mathbf{W}'=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{R}\) also satisfies equation (1), since \(\mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{I}\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{I}\). Different choices of \(\mathbf{R}\) give different “whitenings” with the same covariance. Choosing \(\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{I}\) gives \(\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\) (often called PCA whitening); choosing \(\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{U}^\top\) gives \(\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top\) (ZCA whitening), which stays as close as possible to the original coordinates. Because a rotation does not change any cosine similarity between whitened vectors, both choices give the same pairwise cosines.

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Step 4: dropping directions (Whitening-\(k\))
Let \(\mathbf{W}_k=\mathbf{W}[:,:k]\) be the first \(k\) columns, i.e. \(\mathbf{U}_k\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_k^{-1/2}\). The transformed vectors \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(k)}_i=(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\mathbf{W}_k\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times k}\) have covariance
\[
\mathbf{W}_k^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{W}_k = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_k^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}_k^\top\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{U}_k\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_k^{-1/2} = \mathbf{I}_k,
\]
because \(\mathbf{U}_k^\top\mathbf{U}=[\,\mathbf{I}_k\;\;\mathbf{0}\,]\). So the retained coordinates are still uncorrelated with unit variance. The discarded directions are the ones with the smallest variances \(\lambda_{k+1},\dots,\lambda_d\). Projecting onto the top-\(k\) eigenvectors is exactly PCA, and Whitening-\(k\) is PCA plus rescaling each kept axis by \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_j}\).

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Streaming the mean and covariance
For large corpora we want \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) without holding all vectors in memory. Let \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_n\) be the statistics of the first \(n\) vectors (covariance taken about the running mean, as above). Adding \(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}\):
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n+1} = \frac{n}{n+1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_n + \frac{1}{n+1}\mathbf{x}_{n+1}.
\]
For the covariance, write \(\mathbf{S}_n = n\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_n\). The standard (Welford-style) update is
\[
\mathbf{S}_{n+1} = \mathbf{S}_n + (\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)^\top(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n+1}),
\]
and since \(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n+1}=\frac{n}{n+1}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\), dividing by \(n+1\) gives the exact recursion
\[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n+1} = \frac{n}{n+1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_n + \frac{n}{(n+1)^2}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)^\top(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_n).
\]
We checked this numerically against the batch covariance (agreement to about \(10^{-15}\)). Memory is \(O(d^2)\) regardless of \(N\), and time is \(O(d^2)\) per vector.

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Why this matters for cosine
After whitening, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) no longer contributes a shared offset to dot products, and each (kept) direction contributes equally to \(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}\). That is the “isotropic, so the coordinate formula for cosine is trustworthy” argument of the main article, and also the reason full whitening can hurt: directions with tiny variance, often mostly noise, are given the same weight as the informative ones.

title: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score: The Worked derivation
text:
This is a companion mathematical note to Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers.
When building a subword vocabulary bottom-up, Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) merges whichever adjacent pair \((a, b)\) has the highest raw count \(\text{count}(ab)\). WordPiece (Schuster & Nakajima, 2012; Devlin et al., 2019) instead chooses the merge that best improves the log-likelihood of the training corpus.
In many tutorials, you will usually see two different formulas for WordPiece:
Two questions naturally arise when looking at these equations:
Below is the complete derivation answering both questions from first principles.

title: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score: The Worked derivation
text:
1. The Unigram Log-Likelihood Setup
Suppose our training corpus currently consists of a sequence of \(N\) tokens \(t_1, t_2, \dots, t_N\) drawn from a vocabulary \(V\).
To score how well the vocabulary \(V\) models the corpus, WordPiece fits a unigram language model: it assumes every token occurs independently with its maximum-likelihood probability \(P(t) = \frac{c_t}{N}\), where \(c_t = \text{count}(t)\) is the number of times token \(t\) appears in the corpus.
The total log-likelihood of the corpus is:
\[\log L = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log P(t_i) = \sum_{t \in V} c_t \log \left(\frac{c_t}{N}\right) = \left(\sum_{t \in V} c_t \log c_t\right) - N \log N\]
Now suppose we consider merging every adjacent pair \((a, b)\) (assuming \(a \neq b\)) into a single new token \(ab\), which occurs \(c_{ab} = \text{count}(ab)\) times. Look carefully at what happens to the corpus statistics before and after the merge:

Notice that merging \((a, b) \to ab\) does not just replace \(c_{ab}\) pairs of \((a, b)\) in isolation:

Leftover \(a\)’s and \(b\)’s lose probability mass: Any unmerged instances of \(a\) and \(b\) sitting elsewhere in the corpus see their counts drop from \(c_a \to c_a - c_{ab}\) and \(c_b \to c_b - c_{ab}\).
The entire corpus shrinks: Every merged pair reduces the total token count of the corpus by \(1\), shrinking the corpus size from \(N\) to \(N - c_{ab}\) and slightly boosting the probability \(\frac{c_t}{N - c_{ab}}\) of every other token in the vocabulary.

title: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score: The Worked derivation
text:
2. The Exact Log-Likelihood Change (\(\Delta \log L\))
Let us compute the exact difference \(\Delta \log L = \log L_{\text{new}} - \log L_{\text{old}}\). When we subtract \(\log L_{\text{old}}\) from \(\log L_{\text{new}}\), the \(c_t \log c_t\) terms for all unrelated tokens (\(t \notin \{a, b, ab\}\)) cancel out completely because their counts do not change:
\[\Delta \log L = c_{ab} \log c_{ab} + (c_a - c_{ab})\log(c_a - c_{ab}) + (c_b - c_{ab})\log(c_b - c_{ab}) - c_a \log c_a - c_b \log c_b - (N - c_{ab})\log(N - c_{ab}) + N \log N\]
By splitting \(c_a = c_{ab} + (c_a - c_{ab})\), \(c_b = c_{ab} + (c_b - c_{ab})\), and \(N = c_{ab} + (N - c_{ab})\), we can rearrange this exact equality into three interpretable pieces:
\[\Delta \log L = \underbrace{c_{ab} \log \left( \frac{N \cdot c_{ab}}{c_a \, c_b} \right)}_{\text{Term 1: Primary PMI Gain}} + \underbrace{(c_a - c_{ab}) \log \left( 1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{c_a} \right) + (c_b - c_{ab}) \log \left( 1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{c_b} \right)}_{\text{Term 2: Penalty on leftover } a\text{'s and } b\text{'s}} - \underbrace{(N - c_{ab}) \log \left( 1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{N} \right)}_{\text{Term 3: Corpus shrinkage boost}}\]

Numerical Verification on a Toy Corpus
Suppose \(N = 1000\), \(c_a = 100\), \(c_b = 100\), and \(c_{ab} = 50\) (using natural logarithms \(\ln\)):

Term 1 (Textbook approximation): \(50 \ln\left(\frac{1000 \cdot 50}{100 \cdot 100}\right) = 50 \ln(5) \approx \mathbf{+80.47}\)
Term 2 (Leftover \(a\) and \(b\) penalty): \(50 \ln(1 - 0.5) + 50 \ln(1 - 0.5) = 100 \ln(0.5) \approx \mathbf{-69.31}\)
Term 3 (Corpus shrinkage boost from \(N=1000 \to 950\)): \(-950 \ln(1 - 0.05) \approx \mathbf{+48.73}\)
Exact \(\Delta \log L\): \(80.47 - 69.31 + 48.73 = \mathbf{+59.89}\)

Notice how Term 2 (negative) and Term 3 (positive) pull in opposite directions and partially cancel each other out.

title: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score: The Worked derivation
section: 3. Why Terms 2 and 3 Can Be Ignored (First-Order Taylor Expansion)
text:
3. Why Terms 2 and 3 Can Be Ignored (First-Order Taylor Expansion)
To see why Term 1 dominates in any realistic training corpus, we apply the first-order Taylor expansion for natural logarithms around \(x = 0\):
\[\ln(1 - x) \approx -x \quad \text{for small } x\]

Expanding Term 3 (The Corpus Shrinkage Boost)
In a real training corpus, \(N\) is in the millions or billions while the count of any single candidate pair \(c_{ab}\) is small relative to \(N\) (\(c_{ab} \ll N\)). Setting \(x = \frac{c_{ab}}{N}\) gives:
\[-(N - c_{ab}) \ln \left( 1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{N} \right) \approx -(N - c_{ab}) \left( -\frac{c_{ab}}{N} \right) = c_{ab} - \frac{c_{ab}^2}{N} \approx \mathbf{+c_{ab}}\]


Expanding Term 2 (The Leftover \(a\) and \(b\) Penalty)
Consider the penalty for leftover standalone \(a\)’s, \((c_a - c_{ab}) \ln \left( 1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{c_a} \right)\), across its two boundary regimes:

When \(c_{ab} \ll c_a\): Applying \(\ln(1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{c_a}) \approx -\frac{c_{ab}}{c_a}\) gives \((c_a - c_{ab})(-\frac{c_{ab}}{c_a}) \approx \mathbf{-c_{ab}}\) (and similarly \(\mathbf{-c_{ab}}\) for \(b\)).
When \(c_{ab} \to c_a\): Almost every instance of \(a\) is absorbed into \(ab\), so \((c_a - c_{ab}) \to 0\) and the penalty vanishes to \(\mathbf{0}\).

Across the entire valid domain \(0 \le c_{ab} \le \min(c_a, c_b)\), the combined penalty in Term 2 is strictly bounded between \(-2c_{ab}\) and \(0\).


Dominant Balance
Summing Term 2 (\(\in [-2c_{ab}, 0]\)) and Term 3 (\(\approx +c_{ab}\)) produces a net linear correction bounded inside \([-c_{ab}, +c_{ab}]\). Factoring \(c_{ab}\) out of the entire exact equation yields:
\[\Delta \log L = c_{ab} \cdot \left[ \underbrace{\ln \left( \frac{N \cdot c_{ab}}{c_a \, c_b} \right)}_{\text{PMI of } a \text{ and } b} + \underbrace{\mathcal{O}(1)}_{\text{bounded in } [-1,\,+1]} \right]\]
Because \(N\) is massive, the logarithmic ratio \(\ln\left(\frac{N \cdot c_{ab}}{c_a c_b}\right) = \ln \frac{P(ab)}{P(a)P(b)}\) dominates the bounded \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) offset. Dropping that offset gives the classic first-order approximation:
\[\Delta \log L \approx c_{ab} \cdot \log \frac{P(ab)}{P(a)\,P(b)}\]

title: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score: The Worked derivation
section: 4. From Total Gain to the Simplified Score (Average Gain per Occurrence)
text:
4. From Total Gain to the Simplified Score (Average Gain per Occurrence)
If we rank candidate merges directly by \(\Delta \log L \approx c_{ab} \cdot \log \frac{P(ab)}{P(a)P(b)}\), notice that \(c_{ab}\) sits outside the logarithm as a linear multiplier. Because a linear factor grows much faster than a logarithm, raw pair frequency (\(c_{ab}\)) will still dominate the ranking making the merge order behave almost identically to BPE.
Furthermore, as long as \(c_{ab}\) sits in front of the logarithm, we cannot algebraically drop the \(\log\) or \(N\), because bringing \(c_{ab}\) inside the logarithm turns it into an exponent: \(\log\left(\left(\frac{N \cdot c_{ab}}{c_a c_b}\right)^{c_{ab}}\right)\).
Instead, simplified WordPiece shifts the objective from total corpus log-likelihood gain (\(\Delta \log L\)) to average log-likelihood gain per merge occurrence by dividing both sides by \(c_{ab}\):
\[\frac{\Delta \log L}{c_{ab}} \approx \log \frac{P(ab)}{P(a)\,P(b)}\]
In information theory, this quantity is the Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) between \(a\) and \(b\). Substituting \(P(t) = \frac{c_t}{N}\) gives:
\[\frac{\Delta \log L}{c_{ab}} \approx \log \left( N \cdot \frac{c_{ab}}{c_a \, c_b} \right)\]
Now we can apply two lossless monotonic simplifications to rank candidate pairs:

Drop \(\log(\cdot)\): Because the logarithm is a strictly increasing function, \(\log(x_1) > \log(x_2) \iff x_1 > x_2\) for all positive \(x_1, x_2\).
Drop \(N\): At any given step of the merge loop, the total token count \(N\) is an identical positive constant for every candidate pair \((a, b)\).

Stripping away \(\log\) and \(N\) preserves the exact ranking order of \(\frac{\Delta \log L}{c_{ab}}\) and yields the standard WordPiece scoring rule:
\[\text{score}(a,b) = \frac{c_{ab}}{c_a \cdot c_b} = \frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a) \cdot \text{count}(b)}\]

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
A language model never sees text. It sees a sequence of integers. The component that turns text into those integers (and back) is the tokenizer, and its design quietly shapes cost, context length, multilingual quality and even arithmetic ability.
This article covers the one idea behind almost every modern tokenizer, subword tokenization, with Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) as the main example. We build it by hand, implement it in about 40 lines of Python, then look at its cousins (WordPiece, Unigram), the byte-level trick that removes “unknown” tokens, and the special tokens that structure chat prompts.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
section: 1. Why not characters, and why not words?
text:
1. Why not characters, and why not words?
Pick a granularity for the pieces (“tokens”) the model reads. There are three obvious options, and two of them fail in opposite directions.

Whole words. The vocabulary must contain every word the model might meet. Real text keeps producing new ones: names, typos, product codes, and in languages like German, compounds such as Abwasserbehandlungsanlage (“sewage water treatment plant”). A word-level model maps anything outside its vocabulary to a single <unk> placeholder and loses the information.
Characters. Nothing is ever unknown, but sequences get long. A transformer’s self-attention compares every position with every other, so its cost grows with \(n^2\), where \(n\) is the sequence length in tokens. Longer sequences also push related pieces of information further apart.
Subwords. Frequent words stay whole; rare words are assembled from smaller pieces the model has seen before.

Sennrich et al. (2016) measured this trade-off on a German training corpus of about 100 million words:

Characters make the text 5.5× longer, which for a transformer means roughly \(5.5^2 \approx 30\times\) more attention work. Words need a vocabulary 28× bigger than BPE’s. BPE sits in the middle: it turns the same text into only about 12% more tokens than word-level splitting (112M vs 100M), with a vocabulary small enough to fit in an embedding table.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
2. BPE by hand
BPE comes from data compression (Gage, 1994): repeatedly replace the most frequent pair of adjacent bytes with a new, unused byte. Sennrich et al. adapted it to words: repeatedly merge the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols into one new symbol.
The learning loop:

Start with a vocabulary of single characters. Write every word in the corpus as a sequence of characters.
Count every adjacent pair of symbols, weighted by how often each word occurs.
Merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol, add it to the vocabulary, and rewrite the corpus.
Repeat steps 2–3 for \(k\) merges.






flowchart LR
    A["Corpus as<br/>characters"] --> B["Count adjacent<br/>pairs (weighted)"]
    B --> C["Pick the most<br/>frequent pair"]
    C --> D["Merge it into a<br/>new symbol"]
    D --> E["Rewrite corpus,<br/>record the merge"]
    E -->|"fewer than k merges"| B
    E -->|"k merges done"| F["Output: base symbols<br/>+ ordered merge list"]







A tiny corpus
Word counts: hug ×10, pug ×5, pun ×12, bun ×4, hugs ×5. The base vocabulary is the seven characters b g h n p s u.
Merge 1. Pair counts: u g = 10 + 5 + 5 = 20, p u = 5 + 12 = 17, u n = 12 + 4 = 16, h u = 15, g s = 5, b u = 4. Winner: u g → ug.
After rewriting, the corpus is h ug ×10, p ug ×5, p u n ×12, b u n ×4, h ug s ×5.
Merge 2. Counts are recomputed on the rewritten corpus. pug is now p ug, so it no longer contributes to p u, which drops from 17 to 12. Now u n = 16 is the top pair → un.
Merge 3. h ug = 10 + 5 = 15 wins → hug.

Merging adds a symbol; it does not remove the old ones. u and g stay in the vocabulary (they still appear on their own in pun and bun). So the final vocabulary is
\[|V| = |V_0| + k\]
where \(|V|\) is the final vocabulary size, \(|V_0|\) is the number of starting symbols (here 7), and \(k\) is the number of merges (here 3), giving 10 symbols. The merge count \(k\) is the algorithm’s only hyperparameter.


Using the merges on new text
Learning produces an ordered list of merges. To tokenize any word, split it into characters, then replay the merges in the order they were learned.





flowchart LR
    W["bugs"] --> S["b · u · g · s"]
    S -->|"merge 1: u+g"| M1["b · ug · s"]
    M1 -->|"merge 2: u+n"| M2["no match"]
    M2 -->|"merge 3: h+ug"| M3["no match"]
    M3 --> R["tokens: b, ug, s"]






bugs never appeared in training, yet it becomes b, ug, s, all known symbols. That is the “open vocabulary” property: any word made of known characters can be encoded.
Two details from the original paper:

Merges never cross word boundaries, so the algorithm runs on a word-frequency dictionary, which is much faster than scanning raw text.
Sennrich et al. added a special end-of-word symbol to each word so the original spacing can be restored after translation. Other tokenizers use other conventions (a leading-space marker, or a continuation marker such as ##), but the goal is the same: be able to reconstruct the text exactly.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
3. When characters themselves are unknown
Try mug with our merges. The letter m was never in the corpus, so it is not in the base vocabulary, and the tokenizer can only emit <unk> for it. The original paper notes this limitation: the only symbols unknown at test time are unseen characters, or symbols whose every occurrence in the training text was merged into larger ones. The second case is rarer. A symbol can stay in the merge list but vanish from the segmented training text. Our toy shows the same thing. After five merges the segmented corpus is hug ×10, pug ×5, pun ×12, b un ×4, hug s ×5. The symbol ug is still in the merge list (it was merge 1), so it counts towards the vocabulary size. But in the segmented text it never stands alone: every ug now sits inside hug or pug. A network trained on this text gets no training examples for ug by itself. Yet a new word like bug is split by replaying the merges into b + ug, which hands the network a symbol it has never seen on its own. In practice the paper left such infrequent subword units out of the network’s vocabulary, so such a symbol is simply unknown to the model. The paper’s own example is safeguar, which only ever occurred inside safeguard. The authors saw no such cases at test time, and note they could be fixed by undoing specific merges.
Unicode contains well over a hundred thousand characters, so a base vocabulary of “every character” is large and still incomplete. Byte-level BPE fixes this by starting from bytes instead of characters. Every string, in any script, is a sequence of UTF-8 bytes, so a base vocabulary of just 256 entries can encode anything and unknown tokens become impossible. GPT-2 popularised this: its vocabulary of 50,257 entries is 256 byte tokens, 50,000 learned merges and one special end-of-text token.
The cost is that non-Latin text starts out longer. In UTF-8, é takes 2 bytes, an emoji 4 bytes, and the Hindi word नमस्ते (6 characters) takes 18 bytes. Until merges cover those byte patterns, such text costs many more tokens than English. We come back to this below.
A related fix is byte fallback in SentencePiece-style tokenizers: keep a normal character vocabulary, and decompose rare characters into byte tokens only when needed.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
4. The cousins: WordPiece and Unigram
BPE is not the only way to choose a subword vocabulary. Two others are also worth knowing atleast at the intuition level.
WordPiece (Schuster & Nakajima, 2012; used by BERT, Devlin et al., 2019) also grows its vocabulary bottom-up, but chooses merges by their effect on the likelihood of the training data, not by raw count. The original criterion is the total likelihood gain. The version taught in most tutorials is a simplification that ranks pairs by the gain per occurrence (see the complete mathematical derivation here).
In practice, that reduces to ranking candidate pairs \((a, b)\) by
\[\text{score}(a,b) = \frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a)\,\cdot\,\text{count}(b)}\]
where \(\text{count}(ab)\) is how often \(a\) and \(b\) occur side by side as a pair, and \(\text{count}(a)\), \(\text{count}(b)\) are how often each piece occurs anywhere in the corpus.
Why the denominator matters. Notice that we can rewrite the score as \(\frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a)} \cdot \frac{1}{\text{count}(b)}\), where \(\frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a)}\) is basically \(P(b \text{ follows } a \mid a \text{ just appeared})\). Let’s consider a pair of very common letters like e and s and let’s say, \(\text{count}(es) = 1{,}000\), \(\text{count}(e) = 20{,}000\) and \(\text{count}(s) = 15{,}000\). That means only \(5\%\) of e’s are actually followed by s, and the huge denominator (\(20{,}000 \times 15{,}000\)) pushes the score down to \(3.3 \times 10^{-6}\). Conversely, q and u might only appear together \(150\) times, but almost every q is followed by u (\(\text{count}(q) = 150\), \(\text{count}(u) = 3{,}000\)), giving a score of \(3.3 \times 10^{-4}\), which is a hundred times higher despite being seven times rarer. While BPE merges the most frequent neighbours first, WordPiece merges the most mutually predictive (“sticky”) neighbours first.
At encoding time, rather than replaying a merge list, WordPiece splits each word greedily by matching the longest known vocabulary entry from left to right.
Unigram LM (Kudo, 2018) works top-down. Start with a very large candidate vocabulary and prune. It assumes each subword occurs independently, so a segmentation \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_M)\) of a sentence has probability
\[P(\mathbf{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^{M} p(x_i)\]
where \(M\) is the number of pieces and \(p(x_i)\) is the probability of piece \(x_i\). The best segmentation is the one with the highest \(P(\mathbf{x})\). Training repeatedly estimates the probabilities \(p(\cdot)\), measures how much the total likelihood would drop if each piece were removed, and discards the least useful ones. A side effect is that Unigram can output several plausible segmentations with probabilities, which Kudo used as a regulariser during training.
SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018) is a library, not an algorithm: it can train either BPE or Unigram models, and it treats whitespace as an ordinary symbol so it needs no language-specific pre-splitting.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
5. Practical consequences
Vocabulary size is a trade-off, not a constant. A larger vocabulary shortens sequences (cheaper, more text fits in context because it possesses specific tokens for many whole words) but makes the embedding table and output layer bigger and gives rare tokens fewer training examples. Real systems range from about 30K (BERT) to 128K (Llama 3) and beyond. Sennrich et al. themselves describe their choice of vocabulary size as “somewhat arbitrary”.
Fertility. The fertility of a tokenizer on a text is the average number of tokens per word:
\[f = \frac{\text{number of tokens}}{\text{number of words}}\]
The minimum is \(f = 1\), meaning every word is a single token. Higher is worse: more tokens means a higher bill, less room in the context window and more latency. Rust et al. (2021) show fertility rising sharply for languages that are poorly covered by a tokenizer’s vocabulary. The Llama 3 report quotes an average compression gain on English from 3.17 to 3.94 characters per token versus Llama 2, which is the same idea measured the other way around.
Numbers. A plain BPE vocabulary can split numbers inconsistently (“2024” might be one token while “2025” is two), which hurts arithmetic because digits no longer line up by place value. Tokenizers address this differently. Per a Hugging Face write-up on the topic, Llama 1/2 split every number into single digits, while Llama 3 groups digits in chunks of up to three. There is no single right answer; the point is that the choice is made in the tokenizer, before the model ever trains.
Code. Indentation and repeated whitespace can burn many tokens unless the vocabulary contains merged whitespace pieces. Code-heavy training data usually leads to those being learned.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
6. Special tokens and chat templates
Some vocabulary entries are not learned from text. Special tokens are reserved symbols that carry structure, not language. They must stay atomic: the tokenizer must never split them into characters.







Token (typical role)
Purpose




Beginning-of-sequence (BOS)
Marks where a sequence starts


End-of-sequence (EOS)
The model emits it to say “I’m done”; generation stops when it appears


Padding (PAD)
Fills shorter sequences in a batch to equal length; masked out of attention


Role markers
Mark who is speaking (system, user, assistant) in chat models



Not every tokenizer has all of them. GPT-2, for instance, has exactly one special token, end-of-text.
Chat models are trained on conversations flattened into one token stream with role markers. A purely illustrative example (real markers differ between model families):
<|system|> You are a helpful assistant. <|end|>
<|user|> Explain BPE in one sentence. <|end|>
<|assistant|>
The model then continues from <|assistant|> until it emits its end-of-turn token. Because every family uses different markers, never hand-build these strings. Use the tokenizer’s own chat template (shown below). It is also why EOS matters so much: a model that cannot emit its stop token keeps generating until a length limit cuts it off.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
7. Code

BPE from scratch
from collections import Counter

def get_pair_counts(corpus):
    """corpus: {tuple_of_symbols: count} -> Counter of adjacent pairs."""
    pairs = Counter()
    for symbols, freq in corpus.items():
        for a, b in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
            pairs[(a, b)] += freq
    return pairs

def apply_merge(corpus, pair):
    """Replace every adjacent occurrence of `pair` with the merged symbol."""
    merged = pair[0] + pair[1]
    new_corpus = {}
    for symbols, freq in corpus.items():
        out, i = [], 0
        while i < len(symbols):
            if i < len(symbols) - 1 and (symbols[i], symbols[i + 1]) == pair:
                out.append(merged); i += 2
            else:
                out.append(symbols[i]); i += 1
        key = tuple(out)
        new_corpus[key] = new_corpus.get(key, 0) + freq
    return new_corpus

def train_bpe(word_counts, num_merges):
    corpus = {tuple(w): c for w, c in word_counts.items()}
    base_vocab = sorted({ch for w in word_counts for ch in w})
    merges = []
    for _ in range(num_merges):
        pairs = get_pair_counts(corpus)
        if not pairs:
            break
        best, count = pairs.most_common(1)[0]   # ties: first pair seen wins
        corpus = apply_merge(corpus, best)
        merges.append((best, count))
    return base_vocab, merges

def encode(word, merges, base_vocab):
    """Split into characters, then replay the merges in learned order."""
    symbols = tuple(word)
    for pair, _ in merges:
        symbols = next(iter(apply_merge({symbols: 1}, pair)))
    return [s if (len(s) > 1 or s in base_vocab) else "<unk>" for s in symbols]

counts = {"hug": 10, "pug": 5, "pun": 12, "bun": 4, "hugs": 5}
base, merges = train_bpe(counts, 3)
for pair, c in merges:
    print(pair, c)
print(encode("bugs", merges, base))   # ['b', 'ug', 's']
print(encode("mug", merges, base))    # ['<unk>', 'ug']
Output:
('u', 'g') 20
('u', 'n') 16
('h', 'ug') 15
['b', 'ug', 's']
['<unk>', 'ug']
Real implementations add the pieces we skipped: an end-of-word or leading-space convention, byte-level base symbols, and incremental pair-count updates instead of recounting the corpus on every merge.


A real tokenizer with Hugging Face transformers
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")        # byte-level BPE, 50,257 entries

text = "Tokenization is unbelievably useful."
ids = tok.encode(text)
print(ids)                                          # integer IDs
print(tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(ids))               # the subword pieces
assert tok.decode(ids) == text                      # lossless round trip

# Chat models ship their own template; use it instead of hand-built strings.
chat_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("<a-chat-model-name>")
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain BPE in one sentence."}]
prompt = chat_tok.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True
)
print(prompt)                                       # shows the model's real markers
Run it with a few of your own sentences, including another language and some code, and compare token counts. Seeing the pieces is the fastest way to build intuition.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
8. Common pitfalls

Tokens are not words. English averages a bit over one token per word, but the ratio varies a lot by language and domain. Estimate cost and context use in tokens, never in words.
The tokenizer belongs to the model. IDs only mean something to the vocabulary and embedding table they were trained with. Swapping tokenizers without retraining breaks the model silently.
Whitespace is part of the token. In many tokenizers hello and hello (with a leading space) are different tokens. A stray trailing space in a prompt can change what the model sees.
Unknown characters. A character-level base vocabulary can emit <unk> and lose information. Byte-level BPE avoids this, at the cost of longer sequences for scripts that UTF-8 encodes in several bytes.
Inconsistent number splitting. Do not assume digits are tokenized the same way across models or even across similar numbers. Check before trusting a model on arithmetic or on parsing numeric IDs.
Reading a high fertility as “the model is bad at this language”. It is a symptom of tokenizer coverage, and it directly raises cost and shrinks effective context. Measure it on your own text.
Hand-writing chat templates. A single wrong role marker or missing end-of-turn token can degrade output with no error. Use the template that ships with the tokenizer.
Letting user text become control tokens. If user-supplied text containing a special-token string is parsed as the real special token, it can corrupt the prompt structure. Treat user text as plain text.
Adding new special tokens and expecting them to work. Tokens added after pretraining get embeddings that are untrained until fine-tuning teaches the model what they mean.
Mismatched tokenization between training stages. Anything that compares two models’ token probabilities (as RL fine-tuning methods do) requires both to use identical tokenization and special-token handling.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
Takeaways

Models read integers; the tokenizer is the translation layer and it is learned from data.
Subwords give a middle path: short sequences and an open vocabulary.
BPE learns an ordered list of merges. Learn by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair (recounting each time), encode by replaying the merges in order.
Vocabulary size = base symbols + merges.
Byte-level BPE guarantees no unknown tokens; special tokens add structure; and tokenizer choices, from vocabulary size to digit handling, directly affect cost and capability.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Embeddings are used through geometry: nearest neighbours, clusters, cosine scores. That only works if the geometry is well behaved. This article explains one specific way it often is not (anisotropy), what the research found about it in popular models, and a simple linear fix (whitening) with its dimensionality-reduction variant.
It builds on From Token IDs to Vectors, which introduced embeddings and cosine similarity. The algebra behind the whitening matrix is in a companion derivation page.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
What cosine similarity quietly assumes
Cosine similarity compares directions:
\[
\cos(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i y_i}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{d} y_i^2}}
\]
where \(x_i, y_i\) are the coordinates of the two vectors and \(d\) is the dimension. The formula is written in terms of coordinates, so it measures a geometric angle only if the coordinate axes are a standard orthonormal basis (perpendicular, unit length). Su et al. (2021) use this as a heuristic motivation: if a set of vectors is isotropic, it is reasonable to treat the axes as a good orthonormal basis and trust the formula; if it is not, transform it first and then take cosines. This is a motivating argument and the paper backs it with experiments.

Why non-orthonormal axes break the formula
Suppose our embedding coordinates \((x_1, x_2)\) and \((y_1, y_2)\) are measured along two basis vectors \(\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2\) that are neither perpendicular nor unit-length:
\[
\mathbf{x} = x_1 \mathbf{b}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{b}_2, \qquad \mathbf{y} = y_1 \mathbf{b}_1 + y_2 \mathbf{b}_2
\]
Taking the true geometric inner product \(\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle\) expands into four terms, collected by the Gram matrix \(\mathbf{G}_{ij} = \langle \mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{b}_j \rangle\):
\[
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle = x_1 y_1 \|\mathbf{b}_1\|^2 + x_2 y_2 \|\mathbf{b}_2\|^2 + (x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1)\langle \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \rangle = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{G} \mathbf{y}
\]
The standard cosine formula \(\frac{\sum x_i y_i}{\|\mathbf{x}\|\|\mathbf{y}\|}\) silently assumes \(\|\mathbf{b}_1\| = \|\mathbf{b}_2\| = 1\) and \(\langle \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \rangle = 0\) (i.e., \(\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{I}\)). When the embedding space is anisotropic, meaning it is stretched along certain directions (\(\|\mathbf{b}_i\| \neq 1\)) or correlated across dimensions (\(\langle \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \rangle \neq 0\)), the naive coordinate sum drops the cross-terms and misweights the axes.
This is why Su et al. (2021) apply a whitening transformation \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\mathbf{W}\) before computing cosine similarity: whitening forces the empirical covariance to the identity matrix, effectively rotating and rescaling the coordinate axes back into an orthonormal basis where \(\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{I}\).

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Isotropic vs anisotropic
A set of vectors is isotropic if its directions are spread uniformly, with no preferred direction. A practical test (used by Ethayarajh, 2019, following Arora et al., 2017): the average cosine similarity between randomly sampled pairs. For an isotropic set it is about 0. The closer it is to 1, the more anisotropic the set, which geometrically means the vectors sit in a narrow cone.



Isotropic vs anisotropic embedding spaces, and what whitening does.


There are two ingredients that make a cloud of vectors look like that cone:

A shared offset: all vectors have a large common component (a non-zero mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\)).
Unequal spread: a few directions have much more variance than the rest. Instead of forming a round sphere, the cloud is stretched into a long cigar (ellipsoid). For example, if the first coordinate typically ranges around \(\pm 100\) while the other \(767\) coordinates range around \(\pm 0.1\), that single high-variance axis dominates \(\sum x_i y_i\), effectively reducing a \(768\)-dimensional comparison to a \(1\)-dimensional check.

Whitening, as we will see, targets both.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
What the evidence says: Ethayarajh (2019)
Ethayarajh studied hidden-layer representations (not just the input embedding table) of ELMo (2 layers), BERT-base-cased and GPT-2 (12 layers each), plus each model’s input layer as “layer 0”. Input sentences came from the SemEval Semantic Textual Similarity tasks (2012 to 2016), and only words appearing in at least 5 distinct contexts were analysed.
Finding 1: anisotropy is everywhere. In all layers of all three models, average cosine between random words is clearly above 0 (the one exception is ELMo’s input layer, since it generates character-level embeddings without using context). It is generally larger in higher layers. For GPT-2 it is roughly 0.6 in layers 2 to 8 and then climbs; in the last layer, two random words have an average cosine similarity that is almost 1. BERT also generally rises with depth, but with an exception: its penultimate layer is noticeably more anisotropic than its last. (Approximate values here are read off the paper’s Figure 1.)
Finding 2: upper layers are more context-specific. Define, for a word \(w\) occurring in \(n\) contexts, its self-similarity in layer \(\ell\):
\[
\text{SelfSim}_\ell(w) = \frac{1}{n^2 - n} \sum_{j} \sum_{k \ne j} \cos\big(f_\ell(s_j, i_j),\, f_\ell(s_k, i_k)\big)
\]
Here \(f_\ell(s, i)\) is the layer-\(\ell\) representation of the word at position \(i\) in sentence \(s\), so this is the average cosine between the word’s vectors across different contexts. A value of 1 means no context-specificity. Because anisotropy inflates every cosine, the paper subtracts a baseline (the average cosine of random words in that layer):
\[
\text{SelfSim}^*_\ell(w) = \text{SelfSim}_\ell(w) - \text{Baseline}(f_\ell)
\]
After that adjustment, self-similarity drops as layers go up, so representations become more context-specific. Anisotropy and context-specificity grow together; the paper suggests anisotropy is inherent to, or at least a by-product of, contextualization.
Finding 3: context-specificity looks different per model. Using intra-sentence similarity (how close the words in one sentence are to their mean vector), words in the same sentence grow more similar in higher ELMo layers, grow more dissimilar in BERT (while staying more similar than random words), and in GPT-2 are about as similar to each other as random words.
Finding 4: a single static vector explains little. The maximum explainable variance of a word is the fraction of variance in its contextualized vectors explained by their first principal component:
\[
\text{MEV}_\ell(w) = \frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sum_i \sigma_i^2}
\]
where \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots\) are the singular values of the matrix whose rows are the word’s vectors across contexts. It is the best case for replacing all of a word’s contextual vectors with one fixed vector. After subtracting the anisotropy baseline, on average less than 5% of the variance is explained in any layer of any model. Even so, the first principal component of a word’s vectors from the lower layers makes a static embedding that beats GloVe and FastText on many word-similarity benchmarks.
The paper leaves open whether making contextual representations more isotropic (for example with a penalty added to the training objective) would help.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
section: Why a cone hurts similarity search
text:
Why a cone hurts similarity search
Write each vector as the shared offset plus a residual: \(\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{y} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{b}\). Then
\[
\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y} = \lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}\rVert^2 + \boldsymbol{\mu}\cdot(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}) + \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}.
\]
The informative part, how \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) relate, is the last term. When \(\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}\rVert\) is large, the first term dominates and every pair scores near 1: the meaningful differences are squeezed into a tiny range at the top of the scale. That makes scores fragile to noise and awkward to threshold. A fixed cutoff such as “keep results above 0.9” does not repair it, because what moved is the whole scale, not just where you cut it. Similarly, a few very-high-variance directions that carry non-semantic signal can dominate the dot product. Li et al. (2020), cited by Su et al., report for BERT sentence embeddings that word frequency biases the space.
To be precise about the claim: a narrow cone does not mathematically force the ranking to flip. If \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\cdot(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})\) were zero and the residuals had uniform norm and no noisy dominant directions, the \(\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}\rVert^2\) term would just shift the dot product by a constant (and compress cosine similarity monotonically toward 1) without changing which pair is higher. The problem is that real embeddings are not that clean. The empirical evidence shows that raw BERT sentence embeddings compared with cosine do poorly on similarity benchmarks, and removing the anisotropy improves them (numbers below).

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Whitening
Goal: transform the vectors so that their mean is 0 and their covariance matrix is the identity matrix \(\mathbf{I}\) (every direction has variance 1, and no direction is correlated with another). That is what a standard normal distribution looks like.

Intuition in two dimensions
Picture the points as a tilted, stretched ellipse.

Centre it: subtract the mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) so the cloud is around the origin (removes the shared offset).
Rotate it: rotate the axes to line up with the ellipse (this is what the eigenvectors \(\mathbf{U}\) of the covariance do). Now the coordinates are uncorrelated.
Rescale it: squash the long axis and stretch the short one so every axis has variance 1 (divide each by the square root of its variance, \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\)). The ellipse becomes a circle.






flowchart LR
    X["<b>Embeddings</b><br/>x ∈ ℝ<sup>d</sup><br/>N vectors"] --> M["<b>Centre</b><br/>x − μ"]
    M --> R["<b>Rotate to principal axes</b><br/>(x − μ) U"]
    R --> S["<b>Rescale each axis</b><br/>(x − μ) U Λ<sup>−1/2</sup><br/>divide axis j by √λⱼ"]
    S --> Z["<b>Whitened</b><br/>x̃ = (x − μ) W<br/>mean 0, covariance I"]
    S -. "keep first k columns of W" .-> K["<b>Whitening-k</b><br/>x̃ ∈ ℝ<sup>k</sup>, k < d"]








The formulas
Using the notation of Su et al. (row vectors; \(N\) embeddings \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{1\times d}\)):
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{x}_i, \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})
\]
\[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top \quad\text{(SVD / eigendecomposition)}, \qquad
\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}, \qquad
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathbf{W}
\]
Every symbol:

\(\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d}\): the mean embedding. Subtracting it centres the data.
\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\): the covariance matrix; entry \((j,k)\) says how coordinates \(j\) and \(k\) vary together (basically variance of \(\mathbf{x}_j\) and \(\mathbf{x}_k\)).
\(\mathbf{U}\): an orthogonal matrix whose columns are the principal directions (it rotates without stretching, so it preserves distances).
\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\): a diagonal matrix of variances \(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_d>0\) along those directions.
\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\): the diagonal matrix with entries \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_j}\), i.e. “divide each axis by its standard deviation”.
\(\mathbf{W}\): the single \(d\times d\) matrix that does rotate-and-rescale; applying it is one matrix multiply.

In column-vector notation (used in some textbooks), the same transform reads \(\tilde{\mathbf{h}} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top(\mathbf{h}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\); it is the transpose of the row form.
The check that this gives identity covariance is two lines of algebra; see the derivation page. A tiny example: if \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\text{diag}(4, 1)\) then \(\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}\), \(\mathbf{W}=\text{diag}(1/2, 1)\), so the first coordinate is halved (its standard deviation was 2) and the second is left alone: both now have variance 1.


Whitening-\(k\): shrinking the vectors
The values \(\lambda_j\) are sorted from largest to smallest. A direction with tiny \(\lambda_j\) barely varies, so it carries little information. Keeping only the first \(k\) columns of \(\mathbf{W}\) gives vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^{k}\):
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathbf{W}[:, :k]
\]
This is equivalent to PCA (keep the top directions) followed by the per-axis rescaling. Su et al. call it Whitening-\(k\). Because the cost of comparing two vectors grows with their dimension, a smaller \(k\) also means smaller storage and cheaper similarity computation (the paper motivates the faster-retrieval claim this way). \(k\) is a hyperparameter: for most of their tasks, cutting to about a third of the original dimension was near the best.


What it costs
You need \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) (\(1\times d\)) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) (\(d\times d\)) from a representative corpus of \(N\) vectors, a one-time computation of \(O(N\cdot d^2)\). Both can be accumulated incrementally in a single streaming pass (without storing the vectors); the memory needed does not grow with \(N\). At query time whitening is one matrix multiply per vector.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
section: What the experiments show (Su et al., 2021)
text:
What the experiments show (Su et al., 2021)
They evaluate on seven semantic textual similarity sets, reporting Spearman correlation (\(\times 100\)) between the cosine of two sentence embeddings and human similarity scores. Sentence embeddings are the average of BERT’s first and last layers. “Target” means whitening statistics fitted on the unlabeled sentences of the evaluation dataset; “NLI” means fitted on an NLI corpus. The comparison baseline, BERT-flow (Li et al., 2020), is a more complex method that learns a neural-network transformation to a Gaussian.

71.43



So whitening is competitive with the flow method, and cutting 768 to 256 dimensions did not hurt here. Two honest caveats from the same tables:

It is not uniformly better. On SICK-R with BERT-base, raw scores 63.75 while whitening (target) gives 60.6 and whitening-256 (target) gives 62.2.
Gains shrink for models already trained for similarity. For Sentence-BERT trained on NLI data, STS-B goes from 77.63 to 80.50 with target whitening (80.80 at 256 dimensions), with mixed results across other datasets.

The dimension matters: the paper plots score against \(k\) for each task, and the best \(k\) differs by task (for example, SICK-R with BERT-base (NLI) rises to 66.52 at \(k=109\)).

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Try it: a NumPy demo
Synthetic data (our own), designed to be anisotropic: a large shared offset, three huge-variance directions that carry no topic information, and four “topics” hidden in small differences. We measure the average random-pair cosine and a retrieval-style score: for each vector, what fraction of its 10 nearest neighbours (by cosine) share its topic (P@10).
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, n_topics, per_topic = 64, 4, 250

# --- synthetic "anisotropic" embeddings -------------------------------------
# (1) a big shared offset: every vector leans the same way
common = rng.normal(size=d)
common *= 6.0 / np.linalg.norm(common)
# (2) three non-semantic directions with huge variance, the rest tiny
scales = np.concatenate([[4.0, 3.0, 2.0], np.full(d - 3, 0.15)])
# (3) the "semantics": topic centres, small in every direction
centres = rng.normal(size=(n_topics, d)) * 0.3
topic = np.repeat(np.arange(n_topics), per_topic)
X = common + centres[topic] + rng.normal(size=(len(topic), d)) * scales

def unit(A):
    return A / np.linalg.norm(A, axis=1, keepdims=True)

def mean_cosine(A):
    """Average cosine over all pairs of distinct rows."""
    S = unit(A) @ unit(A).T
    n = len(A)
    return float((S.sum() - n) / (n * (n - 1)))

def precision_at_10(Z):
    """Of each vector's 10 nearest neighbours (cosine), what fraction share its topic?"""
    S = unit(Z) @ unit(Z).T
    np.fill_diagonal(S, -np.inf)
    nn = np.argsort(-S, axis=1)[:, :10]
    return float((topic[nn] == topic[:, None]).mean())

def fit_whitening(X, k=None):
    """Su et al. notation (row vectors): x_tilde = (x - mu) @ W, with W = U Lambda^{-1/2}."""
    mu = X.mean(axis=0)
    Xc = X - mu
    cov = Xc.T @ Xc / len(X)             # Sigma = (1/N) sum (x-mu)^T (x-mu)
    U, lam, _ = np.linalg.svd(cov)       # Sigma = U diag(lam) U^T, lam sorted descending
    W = U / np.sqrt(lam)                 # scale column j of U by 1 / sqrt(lam_j)
    return mu, (W if k is None else W[:, :k])

mu, W = fit_whitening(X)
Xw = (X - mu) @ W

print(f"mean cosine, random pairs:  raw {mean_cosine(X):.3f} | whitened {mean_cosine(Xw):.3f}")
print(f"max |Cov(whitened) - I|:    {np.abs(np.cov(Xw, rowvar=False, bias=True) - np.eye(d)).max():.1e}")
print()
print(f"P@10 raw            {precision_at_10(X):.3f}")
print(f"P@10 centred only   {precision_at_10(X - mu):.3f}")
for k in (4, 8, 16, 32, 64):
    mu_k, W_k = fit_whitening(X, k)
    print(f"P@10 whitening-{k:<3}  {precision_at_10((X - mu_k) @ W_k):.3f}")
Output:
mean cosine, random pairs:  raw 0.539 | whitened -0.001
max |Cov(whitened) - I|:    6.2e-15

P@10 raw            0.968
P@10 centred only   0.975
P@10 whitening-4    0.707
P@10 whitening-8    1.000
P@10 whitening-16   0.954
P@10 whitening-32   0.744
P@10 whitening-64   0.563
What to notice:

The average random-pair cosine goes from 0.539 to about 0: isotropy restored, and the covariance of the whitened data is the identity to numerical precision.
On this toy data, the raw ranking is already good (P@10 0.968). Anisotropy does not automatically break retrieval; this matches the point made above.
Full whitening (\(k=64\)) made P@10 worse (0.563). Dividing by \(\sqrt{\lambda_j}\) blows up the directions with almost no variance, which here are mostly noise. Truncating to a small \(k\) fixed it (1.000 at \(k=8\)), and the best \(k\) is data-dependent. This is the same effect the paper’s \(k\)-sweep plots.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Alternatives

All-but-the-top (Mu & Viswanath, 2018): subtract the mean and remove a few of the top principal directions.
BERT-flow (Li et al., 2020): learn an invertible neural network that maps the embedding distribution to a Gaussian.
Regularisation during training (Gao et al., 2019): penalise similarity between word embeddings so the cone widens.
Contrastive fine-tuning, for example SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021): train the encoder directly so that similar texts are close and others are spread out.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Common pitfalls

Fit on a representative corpus. \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) describe your data. Statistics from a different domain can transfer worse (in the paper, target-fitted and NLI-fitted whitening win on different datasets).
Transform queries and documents identically. Use the same stored \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) for both, and rebuild any vector index built on the raw vectors.
Do not whiten blindly to full rank. Small-variance directions get amplified (see the demo). Choose \(k\) on a validation task. If you have fewer vectors than dimensions (\(N<d\)), \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is singular and cannot be inverted, so \(k\) must be below its rank (or add a small constant to the variances).
Expect uneven gains. Models already trained for similarity benefit less, and some datasets get worse.
Do not mix up the settings. Ethayarajh analyses hidden states of language models; Su et al. whiten sentence embeddings built from BERT layers. Neither is the same thing as the input embedding table, nor as a dedicated text-embedding model.
Measure your own baseline. Compute the average random-pair cosine on your data before deciding it is a problem.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
A transformer cannot read text, and it cannot do much with integers either. Before any attention happens, every token ID has to become a vector of real numbers. This article covers that first step: what the embedding layer is, where its numbers come from, and why the shape of the resulting vector space matters for things like retrieval.
This is the follow-up to the tokenization article, which ended at the point where text has become a sequence of integer token IDs.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
Why IDs are not enough
After tokenization, a sentence is a list of integers, for example [791, 4062, 14198]. Those integers are just labels. ID 4062 is not “more” of anything than ID 4061, so feeding them directly to a network would make it learn arithmetic on arbitrary labels.
The classic fix is one-hot encoding: for a vocabulary of size \(|V|\), token \(i\) becomes a vector of length \(|V|\) with a 1 at position \(i\) and 0 everywhere else. That removes the fake ordering, but it has two problems:

It is huge and almost entirely zeros (for \(|V| = 128{,}000\), one token is a 128,000-dimensional vector).
Every pair of distinct tokens is exactly equally far apart. “king” is no closer to “queen” than to “bicycle”, so the encoding carries no notion of similarity.

An embedding replaces this with a short, dense, learned vector, typically a few thousand numbers, where similarity can be expressed by geometry.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
The embedding table
The embedding layer is one matrix:
\[
\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d}
\]

\(|V|\) is the vocabulary size (number of distinct tokens).
\(d\) is the embedding (model) dimension.
Row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{E}\) is the vector for token \(i\).

Embedding a token is just reading its row:
\[
\text{embed}(x_t) = \mathbf{E}[x_t] \in \mathbb{R}^{d}
\]
Here \(x_t\) is the token ID at position \(t\). For a sequence of \(n\) tokens \([x_1, \dots, x_n]\), stacking the rows gives the input to the first transformer layer:
\[
\mathbf{H}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{E}[x_1] \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{E}[x_n] \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}
\]
Two things worth being clear about:

\(\mathbf{E}\) is a set of learned parameters, like any weight matrix. Unlike the tokenizer (which is fixed before training begins), the embedding table starts as random noise. The model stores one \(d\)-dimensional vector per token, and backpropagation adjusts those vectors alongside the rest of the network’s weights.
A lookup is mathematically a one-hot matrix product, which is why it is differentiable. If \(\mathbf{o}_i \in \{0, 1\}^{|V|}\) is the one-hot vector for token \(i\), then \(\mathbf{o}_i^\top \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{E}[i]\). In practice, frameworks skip the wasteful multiplication by zeros and index the row directly in \(O(1)\) time. Because it is equivalent to a linear projection, gradients flow cleanly during the backward pass, and only the rows for tokens present in the current batch receive updates, while the rest of the vocabulary receives a gradient of zero.






flowchart LR
    A["Text<br/>'The cat sat'"] --> B["Tokenizer"]
    B --> C["Token IDs<br/>[x1, x2, x3]"]
    C --> D["Embedding table, E<br/>(|V| x d)<br/>row lookups"]
    D --> E["Embeddings, H0<br/>(n x d)"]
    E --> F["Transformer<br/>layers"]







How big is it?
The table has \(|V| \times d\) numbers. For a configuration like Llama-3-8B (\(|V| = 128{,}256\), \(d = 4{,}096\)):
\[
128{,}256 \times 4{,}096 \approx 525\text{M parameters},
\]
roughly 6.5% of an ~8B-parameter model. The embedding table is a non-trivial slice of the model, and it grows linearly with the vocabulary, which is one reason vocabulary size is a design decision (see the tokenization article).

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
section: Where do the vectors come from?
text:
Where do the vectors come from?
The table starts out random (for example normal or Xavier-style initialisation) and is trained by backpropagation together with the rest of the model. Nobody tells it that “king” and “queen” should be related. So why do related tokens end up close together?
The model is trained to predict the next token. Consider the contexts “The ___ barked at the mailman” and “I took my ___ for a walk”. Tokens that can fill the same slots (dog, puppy, hound) must make the downstream layers produce similar predictions, and the model eventually learns to give them similar vectors. This is the distributional hypothesis, usually quoted as “you shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth, 1957): similar contexts imply similar meaning, so the embedding table compresses that statistical structure into geometry.
Two training details:

Sparse updates on the input side. During a training step, only the rows of tokens that actually appeared in the batch receive gradient through the lookup. A token that is rarely seen gets few updates, so its row stays closer to its random starting point.
Weight tying. At the output, the model must turn a final hidden vector back into a score for every token in the vocabulary. That needs a \(d \times |V|\) matrix. Weight tying reuses the embedding matrix for this:

\[
\mathbf{W}_{\text{head}} = \mathbf{E}^\top
\]
So the logits (the raw scores before softmax) for a final hidden vector \(\mathbf{h}\) are \(\mathbf{h}\,\mathbf{E}^\top\): the model scores each token by how well \(\mathbf{h}\) lines up with that token’s embedding. Tying saves \(|V| \times d\) parameters and ties the “reading” and “writing” vocabularies together. Not every model does it (GPT-2 does; plenty of large models keep separate input and output matrices).
One consequence: with tying, every row of \(\mathbf{E}\) gets gradient from the output softmax, so the sparse-update picture above only describes the input lookup.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
Measuring closeness: cosine similarity
To say two vectors are “close” we usually compare their directions with cosine similarity:
\[
\cos(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert}
\]
It is 1 when the vectors point the same way, 0 when they are orthogonal, and \(-1\) when opposite. Here \(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}\) is the dot product and \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) the vector length.
Early static word vectors (word2vec-style) were shown to capture relationships as directions, the famous \(\vec{\text{king}} - \vec{\text{man}} + \vec{\text{woman}} \approx \vec{\text{queen}}\) (Mikolov et al., 2013). That is a property reported for those models and it is approximate; do not assume an LLM’s raw embedding table reliably does it.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
section: One vector per token is only the starting point
text:
One vector per token is only the starting point
The table gives each token one fixed vector, whatever the sentence. As the vectors pass through the layers they are mixed with context, so the vector for “bank” in “river bank” ends up different from “bank” in “bank loan”. These are the contextualized representations.
How much does context change them? Ethayarajh (2019) measured this for ELMo, BERT and GPT-2. After adjusting for a geometric effect (we discuss next), on average less than 5% of the variance in a word’s contextualized vectors can be explained by a single static vector for that word. So the layers do real work beyond the lookup table.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
A geometry problem: anisotropy
Here is the catch for anyone who wants to use these vectors for similarity search, clustering or recommendation. If vectors were spread evenly over all directions (isotropic), two totally unrelated vectors would have cosine similarity about 0. Ethayarajh found that in practice, contextualized representations are anisotropic: they sit in a narrow cone, so random pairs already have a high cosine similarity. The anisotropy in GPT-2’s final layer is so extreme that any two random words have an almost perfect cosine similarity on average.





flowchart LR
    A["<b>Anisotropic</b><hr/><small>• vectors in a narrow cone<br/>• random pair: cos ≈ 1</small>"] -- "whitening" --> B["<b>Isotropic</b><hr/><small>• directions spread evenly<br/>• random pair: cos ≈ 0</small>"]






A common post-processing fix is whitening: shift the vectors so their mean is zero, then rotate and rescale so every direction has the same spread. In the notation of Su et al. (2021), with \(\mathbf{x}\) an embedding, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) the mean embedding over a corpus, and \(\mathbf{W}\) a matrix computed from the corpus covariance:
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathbf{W}
\]
Keeping only the first \(k\) columns of \(\mathbf{W}\) also shrinks the vectors, which speeds up retrieval. In their experiments on sentence embeddings from BERT (whitening statistics fitted on the unlabeled evaluation sentences), this improved similarity scores on several benchmarks, for example STS-B Spearman correlation 59.04 → 71.34 for BERT-base, and a 768 → 256 dimension cut scored about the same (71.43). Gains are not uniform across datasets; the deep-dive article shows where it did not help.
To dive deeper, see the next article, Anisotropy and Whitening. It covers how isotropy is measured, what Ethayarajh’s experiments show, the derivation of \(\mathbf{W}\), the dimensionality-reduction trade-off, and a runnable demo.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
section: Code: lookup, one-hot equivalence, weight tying
text:
Code: lookup, one-hot equivalence, weight tying
This is a small PyTorch sketch (our own) showing the three ideas above.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

V, d = 1000, 16                      # tiny vocabulary and dimension
emb = nn.Embedding(V, d)             # E: a learned (V x d) parameter matrix

ids = torch.tensor([3, 17, 3])       # a "sentence" of token IDs
H0 = emb(ids)                        # lookup -> shape (3, d)

# Lookup == one-hot @ E
one_hot = F.one_hot(ids, num_classes=V).float()   # (3, V)
assert torch.allclose(H0, one_hot @ emb.weight, atol=1e-6)

# Weight tying: the output head reuses E, so logits = h @ E^T
head = nn.Linear(d, V, bias=False)
head.weight = emb.weight             # same Parameter object: shared, not copied
h_final = torch.randn(3, d)          # stand-in for the final hidden states
logits = head(h_final)               # (3, V), equals h_final @ emb.weight.T

print(sum(p.numel() for p in {id(p): p for p in
          list(emb.parameters()) + list(head.parameters())}.values()))
# prints V*d = 16000, not 2*V*d, because the matrix is shared

cos = F.cosine_similarity(emb.weight[3], emb.weight[17], dim=0)
print(float(cos))                    # random-init rows: near 0 until trained

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
Common pitfalls

Treating the table as “meaning”. It is one context-free vector per token, and tokens are often sub-words, not words. Contextual meaning lives in the later layers.
Rare tokens. Rows for tokens seen rarely get only few updates during training, so their vectors can be poorly trained.
Weight tying and parameter counts. Tying shares one matrix between input and output; check whether a model ties before comparing parameter counts.
Trusting raw cosine similarity from a pretrained model. High baseline similarity between unrelated items is a known effect (as seen above). Check the baseline on your own data, and consider post-processing or an embedding model trained for similarity.
Fitting whitening on too little data. The covariance must be estimated from a representative corpus; see the deep dive.
